848.title: Maddi in the forest
848.hook: Vessantara's wife comes home with fruit to find her children gone (Jataka 547)
848.howItsDone: Where the Vessantara tale is recited aloud, Maddi's chapter may be chanted slowly and with feeling, and audiences listen to it as part of a merit-making festival.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vessantara, read whole: the elephant, the exile, the gifts, the homecoming. Your line: the last life. Today, the scene we left for later.

A basket of fruit, roots and leaves, heavy on her hip. Maddi has been gathering in the forest all day, the way she does every day, so her children will have something to eat when she gets home. The night before, she slept badly, troubled by a frightening dream, and she told her husband about it. He told her not to worry. Now the light is going, and she is late. Something keeps standing in her path.
screen: `A BASKET OF FRUIT.` → `A BAD DREAM.` → `THE LIGHT IS GOING.`

segments.voice: A lion, a tiger and a leopard stand across her road and won't move. The tale tells us what Maddi doesn't know: they're gods in animal shape, holding her back so she can't come home in the middle of the gift. She pleads with them, and only at nightfall do they step aside. Every evening the children run out to meet her. Tonight nobody runs. She calls their names. She looks where they played, by the pond, under the trees. Vessantara, sitting there, at first says nothing. Maddi searches the whole night through, and at dawn she falls at her husband's feet as if dead. He sprinkles water on her face to bring her round, and only then tells her: he has given the children away to a brahmin, so that he might reach awakening. The tale has her rejoice in the gift, and join her merit to his. Some readers find that ending hard to accept. Others hear in it a love already tested by the worst night of her life. The tale does not hurry past her grief. It gives her search room to breathe, line after line, place after place. Tradition says that where the whole tale is recited aloud at festivals, Maddi's search is a part listeners wait for, and weep through. A story told for the sake of generosity stops, for a long time, to stand beside a mother looking for her children in the dark.
screen: `A LION, A TIGER, A LEOPARD.` · `NOBODY RUNS TO MEET HER.` · `SHE SEARCHES ALL NIGHT.` · `SHE REJOICES IN THE GIFT.` · then, large: `MADDI'S GRIEF.`

segments.voice: In Maddi's tale, love looks like worry. Bring to mind a time someone who cared for you worried about you: a night they waited up, a face at the door when you finally got home, and look at it now as care with nowhere else to go. If that relationship is a painful one, choose anyone whose care reached you.
Maddi. The mother who came home with fruit and searched all night for her children. Today's word.
Your line: Maddi's grief. The tale gives her search all the room it needs. Until tomorrow.

849.title: Tales in stone
849.hook: Jataka carvings at Bharhut and Borobudur, paintings on the cave walls at Ajanta
849.howItsDone: Buddhist pilgrims walk around stupas and monuments with the shrine on their right, and at places like Borobudur the carved birth stories line the path they walk.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maddi, searching all night for her children. Your line: Maddi's grief. Today, the tales leave the page.

A stone post, its faces carved with round panels. On one round panel, a deer kneels in front of a king. On another, monkeys cross a river on a bridge made of their own bodies. Next to some of the panels, a few letters are cut into the stone: the name of the tale. Somebody, long ago, wanted to make sure you knew which story you were looking at. This is the railing of a stupa at Bharhut, in India.
screen: `A CARVED STONE POST.` → `A DEER BEFORE A KING.` → `THE TALE'S NAME, CUT IN STONE.`

segments.voice: The carvers at Bharhut didn't only show the tales; on some panels they carved the tale's name beside the picture. So a scene of animals and kings isn't a guess. The stone tells you which birth story it is, and scholars can match it with the tales we still read. On the island of Java stands Borobudur, a huge Buddhist monument built in terraces, its galleries lined with carved panels, among them birth stories. Pilgrims walk around it, keeping the monument on their right, and the stories unfold beside them, scene after scene, climbing level by level. You read it with your feet. In western India, at Ajanta, halls were cut straight into a cliff, and their walls were painted with scenes from the Buddha's lives: a white elephant among lotus pools, a prince and his court, crowds and palaces, all on rock. Why put tales in stone at all? A carving teaches anyone who can see, whether or not they can read. A monk or a parent could stand at a panel and tell the story while pointing to it. And stone lasts. The tales we've been hearing were told aloud and copied, and also cut into rock and painted on walls in places far apart. The six-tusked elephant you met a few days ago stands on a railing at Bharhut and on a painted wall at Ajanta. When you hear a Jataka, you are hearing something people once walked past, touched and pointed at.

850.title: The Jataka, closed
850.hook: the long road of many lives that the Jataka traces to one awakening
850.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use Jataka tales in sermons, schools and festivals, often telling a tale and then explaining which perfection it shows.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Jataka in stone, at Bharhut, Borobudur and Ajanta. Your line: the tales in stone. Today we close the book of birth stories.

An elephant who carries a lost man out of the forest. A woodpecker who pulls a bone from a lion's throat. A treasurer who points at a dead mouse in the street. A caravan leader in the desert. A clever sage at court. A king who gives away his eyes. A prince who gives away everything. In the Jataka, they are all the same one: the bodhisatta, the being on the way to becoming the Buddha.
screen: `AN ELEPHANT, A WOODPECKER, A TREASURER.` → `A SAGE, A KING, A PRINCE.` → `ALL THE SAME ONE.`

segments.voice: Start with how each tale ends. In the Jataka, the Buddha tells a story of the past because of something happening in the present: a monk who's discouraged, a quarrel, a kindness. When the story is done, he names who everyone was. That monk was the frightened deer. That troublemaker was the jackal. And the wise one, he says, was I. That last line turns a fable into a birth story. Under the tales runs a road. Early in these weeks came Sumedha, lying in the mud before an earlier Buddha, setting out on the long way and taking on the perfections he would need. Every tale since has been one step on that road: generosity here, patience there, truthfulness, effort, wisdom. And the bodhisatta isn't always a king or a sage. He's an elephant, a bird, a merchant, a minister. The tales let the one on the way to awakening be an animal or an ordinary worker. The collection closes with Vessantara and the gift that cost him nearly everything. Tradition tells the life after it as the one in which he becomes the Buddha. So the Jataka doesn't end with an awakening. It ends right before one, with a family coming home from the mountain. Some Buddhists read these stories as history, some as teaching tales, some as both. Read either way, the collection tells awakening as a long walk, made of small turns in ordinary lives.

segments.voice: Let the stories of these weeks pass by: the dead mouse, the monkey gardeners, the donkey in the lion's skin, the sky that was falling, the six-tusked elephant, Maddi in the forest. Don't choose the one you think you should; notice which one comes back, and say to yourself, in one sentence, why.

851.title: The first council
851.hook: elders gather at Rajagaha after the Buddha's death: Ananda recites the discourses, Upali the discipline (Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
851.carry: held by many mouths, not just one memory
851.howItsDone: Theravada monks still recite texts together in chanting sessions, and the tradition looks back to this first council as the moment its teachings were gathered and fixed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Jataka, closed: one being, many lives. Your line: many lives, one road. Today a new part begins: what happened after the Buddha was gone.

The Buddha has died, and the monks on the road are weeping. One old monk named Subhadda tells them to stop. Don't grieve, he says. We're rid of that great ascetic who was always telling us what's proper and what isn't. Now we can do as we like. The elder Mahakassapa hears it, and he doesn't forget it. In the Vinaya, the book of monastic discipline, it is this remark that sets him to work. If the teaching isn't gathered now, he reasons, people like Subhadda will decide what it was.
screen: `THE BUDDHA HAS DIED.` → `NOW WE CAN DO AS WE LIKE.` → `KASSAPA REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Mahakassapa proposes that the elders recite the teaching and the discipline together, before anything false can take root. The Vinaya says five hundred elders were chosen to meet at Rajagaha for the rains. One almost wasn't there. Ananda had been at the Buddha's side for years and had heard him teach again and again, but he was not yet fully awakened. The text says he worked hard through the night before the council, and as he lay down to rest, before his head reached the pillow, his mind was freed. He walked into the council as one of the elders. Mahakassapa doesn't ask for speeches. He asks questions, one at a time. To Upali, a former barber who had become an expert in the monastic rules: where was the first rule laid down? About whom? In what case? Upali answers, and the discipline is recited. Then to Ananda: where was this discourse given? To whom? Ananda answers, and the discourses are recited. The Pali name for the gathering is sangiti, a chanting together. It wasn't a debate over new ideas. It was a room full of people saying the same words aloud, checking them against each other, so that the teaching would be held by many mouths and not just one memory. Some scholars ask how much of this account is history and how much is later telling. The tradition remembers it as the moment the teaching was gathered in, so it could be handed on.
screen: `RECITE IT BEFORE IT DRIFTS.` · `ANANDA, AWAKE JUST IN TIME.` · `UPALI ON RULES, ANANDA ON DISCOURSES.` · `A CHANTING TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE FIRST COUNCIL.`

852.title: Carried by memory
852.hook: for a long time, tradition says, the teaching was memorized and chanted by reciters, not written
852.carry: the binding of an unwritten book
852.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, monks and novices learn suttas and verses by heart and chant them together, and some monks learn whole collections.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sangiti, elders reciting the teaching together, question by question. Your line: held by many mouths, not just one memory. Today, what happened to all those words next.
screen: `HELD BY MANY MOUTHS, NOT JUST ONE MEMORY.`

segments.voice: "Thus have I heard." Open the Long Discourses at the beginning and that is how the first sutta starts, and the same words open sutta after sutta. Tradition says the voice is Ananda's, at the council, reciting what he heard the Buddha say. It's a strange way to start a holy text. Not: thus it is. Not: thus it was written. Thus I heard it. The teaching opens by telling you how it reached you: through someone's ears, and someone's memory. Today, how the teaching traveled before it was written down.
screen: `THUS HAVE I HEARD.` → `NOT: THUS IT WAS WRITTEN.` → `THROUGH SOMEONE'S EARS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says that after the council, groups of monks took on different collections of the teaching and learned them by heart, chanting them together and teaching them to their students, who taught their own. A text was not a book on a shelf. It was a group of people who could say it. Read the suttas and you notice the repetition: the same passage again and again, lists of three things, four things, eight things, whole paragraphs repeated with one word changed. On paper, that can feel slow. Out loud, it helps a memory hold its shape. Repetition works like the binding of an unwritten book. The Vinaya tells of an elder named Purana who arrived after the council was over. The elders invited him to accept what they had recited. He said it was well recited, but he would remember the teaching the way he himself had heard it from the Buddha. The text records his answer and moves on. Even in the first generation, memory came in more than one voice. At last, the chronicles of Sri Lanka say, in a time of hardship, monks there wrote the texts down so they would not be lost. Until then, tradition says, they had been carried in people. Heard that way, the long stretch before writing looks less like a gap than a kind of care: the teaching was kept alive by being said aloud, by people who had given their lives to it.

853.title: The minor rules
853.hook: the Buddha allowed minor rules to be dropped, but no one asked which; the elders kept them all
853.howItsDone: Theravada monks keep the full code of monastic rules, minor ones included, and recite it together at regular gatherings of the community.

segments.voice: Yesterday: thus have I heard, a teaching held in people before it was written. Your line: the binding of an unwritten book. Today, one thing nobody remembered to ask.

Which rules are minor? It sounds like a small question. In the account of the Buddha's last days, he tells Ananda that after he is gone, the community may, if it wishes, set aside the lesser and minor rules. It's a generous permission, a teacher loosening his grip and trusting his students. But it comes with a gap in it, and at the first council, the gap opens.
screen: `WHICH RULES ARE MINOR?` → `YOU MAY SET THEM ASIDE.` → `A GAP IN THE PERMISSION.`

segments.voice: At the council, Ananda tells the elders what the Buddha said: the minor rules may be dropped. The elders ask the obvious thing. Which ones? Did you ask him? Ananda says no. He didn't ask. The Vinaya lets us hear the elders trying. Some say every rule except the gravest ones is minor. Others draw the line a little higher, then higher again. Each answer is reasonable. None of them settles it, because the one person who could settle it is gone. Then Mahakassapa turns the question around. Lay people know which things are proper for monks, he says. If we start dropping rules now, they'll say the teacher's rules lasted only as long as the teacher, like smoke. So let us not add rules the Buddha didn't make, and not take away rules he did make. The elders agree. They kept them all. It cost Ananda something. After the council, the elders name several things he did wrong, and failing to ask which rules were minor is one of them. Ananda says he didn't see it as a fault, but out of trust in the elders he acknowledges it. Some readers hear the elders being hard on him. Others hear the community choosing steadiness over its own best guess. Either way, the council kept the whole set of rules, and in the Theravada telling, that is why the small rules are still kept alongside the great ones.

854.title: The second council
854.hook: a hundred years after the Buddha, at Vesali, a dispute over ten points, including handling money (Vinaya, Cullavagga 12)
854.howItsDone: Under the Theravada monastic code, monks are not to accept gold and silver, and lay stewards may look after money given for a monastery.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mahakassapa, and the minor rules nobody dropped. Your line: they kept them all. This week: Maddi's night, tales in stone, the Jataka closed, the first council, memory, and the rules. Today, a rule somebody bent.

A bronze bowl full of water sits in the middle of the gathered monks. It's the observance day in the city of Vesali, and lay people are coming in. The monks ask them to drop coins into the bowl for the community. A visiting monk named Yasa watches this and can't stay quiet. Don't give, he tells the lay people. Gold and silver aren't allowed to monks. The Vinaya says this happened a hundred years after the Buddha's death.
screen: `A BOWL OF WATER, A CITY.` → `COINS FOR THE MONKS.` → `YASA SAYS DON'T GIVE.`

segments.voice: The monks of Vesali don't take Yasa's protest well. They tell him he has insulted the lay people and must go and apologize. He goes, but instead of apologizing, he explains why the Buddha forbade monks to take money. The lay people are persuaded, and they side with him. Now the Vesali monks want him out. Yasa travels to find senior monks, and it turns out the coins are only one of ten practices the Vesali monks have allowed themselves. Most of them sound tiny: carrying salt in a horn so food can be salted later; eating when the sun's shadow has moved two fingers past noon; drinking palm juice that hasn't quite turned to wine; a sitting rug without a fringe. Small loosenings, each one with an argument behind it. Senior monks gather at Vesali. To keep the meeting from turning into a shouting match, they hand the questions to a small panel drawn from both sides. The panel goes through the ten points one at a time, checking each against the rules, and finds every one of them not allowed. In this account, a hundred years in, the hard questions weren't about grand doctrine. They were about salt, sunlight and coins. The elders had promised to keep every rule. Here is what keeping that promise looked like: not a single dramatic heresy, but ten small bends, each one easy to explain, examined one by one.
screen: `APOLOGIZE, OR EXPLAIN?` · `SALT, SHADOWS, PALM JUICE, COINS.` · `A PANEL FROM BOTH SIDES.` · `TEN SMALL BENDS, ONE BY ONE.` · then, large: `THE TEN POINTS.`

segments.voice: Think of one small rule you made for yourself or agreed to, a bedtime, a budget, a promise about your phone, and find where you've let it slide a little. Don't scold; just hear the reason you give yourself clearly, the way the elders heard each point.
Yasa. The visiting monk who objected to coins in the alms bowl, and set off the dispute that led to this council. Today's word.
Your line: the ten points. Each bend came with a reason that sounded fine. That's day eight hundred fifty-four.
